what_its_for: Metoclopramide is used to treat nausea, vomiting, and heartburn. It is also used to help your stomach empty faster if you have a condition called gastroparesis (slow stomach emptying), which is common in people with diabetes. It works by helping food move through your stomach and intestines more quickly.
how_to_take: Take metoclopramide exactly as your doctor tells you. Swallow the regular tablet with a full glass of water. If you have the orally disintegrating tablet (ODT), place it on your tongue and let it dissolve — do not chew or swallow it whole. Take it 30 minutes BEFORE meals and at bedtime, unless your doctor tells you otherwise. Do not take more than your doctor prescribed, and do not take it for longer than 12 weeks unless your doctor specifically directs you to.
dosing: The usual adult dose is 10 mg taken up to 4 times a day (before each meal and at bedtime). Your doctor may start you on a lower dose if you are older or have kidney problems. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions, as doses can vary based on your condition.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is still close to the time you were supposed to take it. If your next scheduled dose is coming up soon, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do NOT double up or take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store metoclopramide at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets. Do not use the medication past the expiration date on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking metoclopramide — it can make drowsiness and dizziness much worse. Do not drive a car, operate heavy machinery, or do anything that requires you to be alert until you know how this medicine affects you. Avoid taking other medications that cause drowsiness, such as sleep aids, anti-anxiety drugs, or other nausea medicines, without checking with your doctor or pharmacist first.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you notice: uncontrolled muscle movements in your face, tongue, or body (such as grimacing, lip smacking, or jerking movements); muscle stiffness or spasms; feeling restless or unable to sit still; a high fever with stiff muscles; confusion; or fast or irregular heartbeat. Also call your doctor if you feel depressed, anxious, or have thoughts of self-harm. Long-term use can cause a serious movement disorder called tardive dyskinesia, which may be permanent — this is why you should not use this medicine for more than 12 weeks unless your doctor says so.
when_it_works: Metoclopramide usually starts working within 30 to 60 minutes after you take a dose. You may begin to feel relief from nausea fairly quickly. For gastroparesis, it may take a few days of regular use before you notice significant improvement in your symptoms.
special_populations: Older adults: Use with caution. Older people are more sensitive to side effects, especially drowsiness and movement problems. Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor before using this medication if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Breastfeeding: Metoclopramide passes into breast milk. Discuss the risks and benefits with your doctor before breastfeeding while on this medication. Kidney or liver problems: Your doctor may need to lower your dose if your kidneys or liver are not working well. Children: Metoclopramide is generally not recommended for children unless specifically prescribed by a pediatric specialist, as they are at higher risk for movement-related side effects.
